title: Pro-Human AI Declaration
content:
AI is already influencing who gets hired, what information we see, and decisions about our health, money and access to essential services.
When these systems get something wrong, companies should not be able to avoid accountability.
That’s why AI experts, technologists, artists, parents, workers, faith leaders and scholars created the Pro-Human AI Declaration — a strong demand that AI companies answer for the systems they build and the decisions those systems make.
By adding your name, you’ll help make this the largest public campaign on AI in history. You’ll help deliver the declaration to governments and company executives around the world and build pressure for clear responsibility, meaningful oversight and real accountability.
Help reach 1 Million signatures and make this the largest public campaign on AI in history!

report.summary: A broad coalition’s Pro-Human AI Declaration demands AI companies be held accountable for high-stakes decisions, aiming for 1 million signatures and global pressure.
report.background: AI now shapes hiring, information exposure, health, finance and access to essential services. As these systems spread, harms from bias, opacity, errors and unaccountable automation have drawn concern from researchers, workers, artists, faith groups and the public. Existing laws often lag behind rapid deployment, and companies can be shielded by terms of service, algorithmic secrecy or fragmented regulation. The Pro-Human AI Declaration emerges from that gap: a cross-sector campaign arguing that firms must answer for the systems they build and the decisions those systems make. It is not a technical standard but a public pressure tool, intended to be delivered to governments and executives worldwide. Its immediate goal is 1 million signatures, framed as the largest public campaign on AI in history, to demand clear responsibility, meaningful oversight and real accountability.
key_points: The declaration’s core demand is simple: when AI systems influence hiring, news, health, money or essential services, companies must not escape accountability. It targets the builders and deployers of algorithmic decision systems, not AI itself. By framing the issue as human welfare versus unaccountable automation, it seeks clear responsibility, oversight and remedies when systems cause harm.

The campaign is backed by a broad coalition of AI experts, technologists, artists, parents, workers, faith leaders and scholars. That mix is meant to show concern crosses political, professional and religious lines. Signatories hope the declaration will be delivered to governments and company executives worldwide, turning public sentiment into pressure for enforceable responsibility.

Organizers aim for 1 million signatures, calling it the largest public campaign on AI in history. Supporters are asked to add their names and share a link, which helps amplify the message. The number is both symbolic and tactical: a large signatory count can attract media attention, influence policymakers and make executives feel reputational risk.

The declaration focuses on accountability and oversight rather than calling for a blanket ban or specific technical fix. It implies companies should be liable for foreseeable harms, provide transparency, and submit to meaningful human review. How that translates into law, audits, liability rules or corporate governance remains dependent on government action and company responses.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the campaign adds reputational and political pressure at a time when regulators are drafting rules and companies are competing on trust. It may accelerate voluntary commitments, transparency reports and third-party audits. For developers, it signals that model accuracy alone is not enough; documentation, testing, monitoring, human review, incident reporting and clear ownership will matter. For regular users, success could mean more recourse when algorithmic decisions go wrong, better explanations and safer services, but a petition alone does not create legal rights. It may shift norms or feed into legislation. Its main impact is likely agenda-setting: making accountability a default expectation rather than an afterthought.
report.tools: To follow up: sign or share the Pro-Human AI Declaration at prohumandeclaration.com and track its signature count. For accountability practice, explore the AI Incident Database, Model Cards and Datasheets for Datasets for documentation, Fairlearn and IBM AI Fairness 360 for bias testing, and the OECD AI Policy Observatory or EU AI Act tracker for regulation. These open resources help developers and advocates turn accountability demands into concrete checks and evidence.
